sections.h2: Who records deeds in Seneca County, Ohio?
sections.html:
The Seneca County Recorder records deeds, mortgages and related land documents for the whole county, and the office sits in the county building at 109 S. Washington Street in Tiffin. The county's published directory lists the Recorder's phone as 419-447-4434. Under Ohio Revised Code 317.13, the recorder enters each instrument in the order it is presented and stamps it with the date and exact time.

Seneca County is in northwestern Ohio. Tiffin is the county seat, and the Sandusky River runs through the county from south to north. Wikipedia puts the county at 553 square miles and about 80 percent of it in agriculture, so many deeds here cover farm ground, rural splits and in-town lots in Tiffin, Fostoria and Bellevue, not only houses on city streets.

A recorded deed is what puts the new owner's name in the public record. If you sell a Seneca County house for cash, the deed is the last paper that matters: until it is stamped by the auditor and recorded, the title company and the buyer's lender cannot show the transfer as complete.

sections.h2: What happens at the Auditor before the Recorder sees my deed?
sections.html:
The deed goes to the Seneca County Auditor first and to the Recorder second. The Auditor's real estate transfer page says all transfer documents must be presented to the Auditor before recording, and that transfers follow Ohio Revised Code 319.203.

The Auditor's office is in the same building, Suite 2206, with a published phone of 419-447-0692 and hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday. The checks go there, not to the Recorder:

  • The conveyance fee for Seneca County is printed as $4.00 per thousand dollars conveyed.
  • The transfer fee is $.50 for each parcel on the deed.
  • Checks are made payable to the Seneca County Auditor. Since January 21, 2022, blank checks are refused, and a wrong amount gets the documents returned unrecorded.
  • The Auditor's site has a conveyance fee calculator and the DTE 100 and DTE 100 (EX) forms.

The statutes behind this are short. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the base conveyance fee at one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater, and section 322.02 lets a county commission add a real property transfer tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars. The county page states the combined local rate as $4.00 per thousand.

sections.h2: Which Seneca County sales skip the conveyance fee?
sections.html:
Some transfers carry no conveyance fee, and the seller or heir files the DTE 100 (EX) form to say why. The exemption list in ORC 319.54(G)(3) is long. These are the ones that come up most often with houses:

  • A gift between spouses, or between a parent and child or the spouse of either.
  • A transfer where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and the transaction is not a gift.
  • A transfer among the heirs or devisees of one decedent when no money is paid for the property.
  • A transfer to the trustee of a trust when the grantor kept an unlimited power to revoke it, and the reverse transfer back to the grantor.
  • A deed made under a court order, to the extent the transfer is not itself a sale carried out under that order.
  • A deed that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded.

An arm's-length sale to an investor or cash buyer does not fit any of these, so the fee applies. Ask the Seneca County Auditor before closing if you think an exemption fits, because the exemption claim is filed with the Auditor on the DTE 100 (EX) form.

sections.h2: What does the deed itself need to say?
sections.html:
The deed must be signed by the grantor and acknowledged before a notary or another officer named in ORC 5301.01, which lists judges and clerks of courts of record, county auditors, county engineers, notaries and mayors. The statute covers deeds, mortgages, land contracts and leases of any interest in real property.

The Seneca County Auditor adds local requirements. A deed needs an accurate legal description and the right parcel numbers, and the description must name the township or city or village, the county and the state. Legal descriptions are checked by the Seneca County Tax Map Office, which the county's directory lists at 419-448-5719, and the text should match the prior deed or the new survey word for word.

Splits take longer. The Auditor's page says a land survey is generally required for a newly split parcel, and approval comes from the Seneca Regional Planning Commission in unincorporated areas, the city engineer inside a city, or village council inside a village. The Auditor's site also announced that, starting January 1, 2027, splits, resurveys and combinations will not show in property tax records until tax year 2028. If part of a lot is being sold, plan the survey first.

sections.h2: How much does the Seneca County Recorder charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
Recording fees are set by ORC 317.32, not by the county. For a standard instrument the statute lists a $17 base fee plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for the first two pages, and $4 plus $4 for each page after that. It also lets a county add a document preservation surcharge of up to $5.

Because the surcharge is optional, the total can differ between counties. Shelby County's published schedule, for example, rose by $5 in 2025. Ask the Seneca County Recorder at 419-447-4434 for the exact per-document total before you mail a check, since a short or over payment can send the deed back.

sections.h2: Can I record or search Seneca County deeds online?
sections.html:
Ohio law pushed county recorders toward online access. ORC 317.13(E) and (F) required each recorder, by June 30, 2026, to offer electronic recording of real property conveyances and to post electronic indexes and images of instruments recorded since January 1, 1980, with no fee for access. That deadline has passed, so ask the Seneca County Recorder how to submit a deed electronically and where the index lives.

The Auditor's real estate page also notes five public computers for records: two in the Auditor's office, two in the Treasurer's office and one in the Recorder's office. The Auditor's site lets you search any parcel to see the appraisal and payment history, and it carries a sales report that helps a seller see what nearby homes have sold for.

sections.h2: What property tax questions come up when a Seneca County house sells?
sections.html:
Property tax is billed by the Seneca County Treasurer and valued by the Auditor, and a closing agent will ask the Treasurer for the payoff on any unpaid half. The Auditor's records show roughly 35,539 parcels in the county.

  • Value appeals go to the county Board of Revision. The Seneca County brochure says complaints are filed after January 1 and on or before March 31 of the following year, with original notarized signatures, and a mailed complaint counts by its U.S. postmark.
  • If you disagree with the Board, the brochure gives 30 days from the mailing of its notice to appeal to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals on Form DTE 4, or you can go to the Seneca County Court of Common Pleas.
  • Homestead applications for seniors and disabled owners are due December 31 of the year they are sought. For 2026 bills the Auditor reported a household income limit of $40,000 for new applicants, with no limit for disabled veterans.

If you inherited the house, the heirs-at-law exemption from the conveyance fee may apply, and the Auditor can tell you which form to file.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Seneca County, Ohio?
faqs.a: At the Seneca County Recorder's office in the county building at 109 S. Washington Street, Tiffin. The deed must be stamped by the Seneca County Auditor first. Call the Recorder at 419-447-4434 to confirm hours and how to submit by mail or electronically.

faqs.q: Does the Auditor or the Recorder collect the transfer fees?
faqs.a: The Auditor collects the conveyance fee and the $.50 per parcel transfer fee, and the Recorder collects the recording fee. The county page prints the conveyance fee as $4.00 per thousand dollars conveyed. They are separate payments to separate offices.

faqs.q: Can the Recorder refuse to record my deed?
faqs.a: Yes, in limited cases. ORC 317.13 lets the recorder refuse an instrument that the Revised Code does not require or authorize to be recorded, or one the recorder has reasonable cause to believe is materially false or fraudulent. A refused filer may ask the common pleas court to order recording.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to transfer a house in Seneca County?
faqs.a: Nothing on the Auditor's page requires one, but the transfer rules are strict about legal descriptions, parcel numbers and signatures, and the Tax Map Office must approve descriptions. Many sellers use a title company or attorney for that reason.

faqs.q: When must I appeal my Seneca County property value?
faqs.a: Between January 1 and March 31 of the year after the tax year in question, using the Board of Revision complaint form. The Seneca County brochure notes the complaint must carry original notarized signatures, and the Auditor at 419-447-0692 can say which reappraisal or update applies to your parcel.
